blocks.body:
Nine people at a party: can each of them shake hands with exactly three others? A road network: is there a round trip that uses every road exactly once? A company of $n$ offices: what is the fewest cables that keep them all connected? Each question is about a set of objects and a symmetric relation between pairs of them. That structure is a graph.

This lesson sets up the basic vocabulary (degrees, paths, connectivity, trees) and proves the first two real theorems of the subject: the characterisation of trees by their number of edges, and Euler's criterion for a closed walk through every edge.

blocks.title: Graph
blocks.body:
A graph $G = (V, E)$ consists of a finite set $V$ of vertices and a set $E$ of edges, each edge being a set $\{u, v\}$ of two distinct vertices, written $uv$. Then $u$ and $v$ are adjacent, or neighbours, and are the ends of the edge. The degree $\deg v$ of a vertex is the number of edges containing it.

This is a simple graph: no edge joins a vertex to itself, and two vertices are joined at most once. When we need several edges between the same pair (parallel edges) or edges from a vertex to itself (loops, each adding $2$ to the degree) we say multigraph.

blocks.title: Handshake lemma
blocks.body:
In every graph (or multigraph),
$$\sum_{v \in V} \deg v = 2|E|.$$
Consequently the number of vertices of odd degree is even.

Count the pairs $(v, e)$ with $v$ an end of edge $e$ (a loop counted twice). Counting by vertices gives $\sum_v \deg v$; counting by edges gives $2$ for each edge. So the two totals agree. The sum of all degrees is even, and the even degrees contribute an even amount, so the odd degrees must also add up to an even number, which needs an even number of them.

blocks.title: Walks, paths and connectivity
blocks.body:
A walk is a sequence of vertices $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ in which consecutive vertices are adjacent; its length is $k$, the number of steps. A trail is a walk that never uses the same edge twice, and a path is a walk that never visits the same vertex twice. A cycle is a closed walk $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k = v_0$ with $k \ge 3$ whose vertices $v_0, \dots, v_{k-1}$ are distinct.

If there is a walk from $u$ to $v$, there is a path: take a shortest walk from $u$ to $v$; if it visited some vertex twice, cutting out the loop between the two visits would give a shorter walk. A graph is connected if every two vertices are joined by a path. In general, 'joined by a path' is an equivalence relation on $V$, and its classes are the connected components.

Two facts used below. Deleting an edge that lies on a cycle does not disconnect anything, because any path that used the edge $uv$ can detour around the rest of the cycle. And adding an edge between two different components joins them into one without creating a cycle.

blocks.title: Tree
blocks.body:
A tree is a connected graph with no cycles. A leaf is a vertex of degree $1$. A graph with no cycles (each component a tree) is a forest.

Trees are the minimal connected graphs: every edge is needed, since removing any edge of a tree disconnects it.

blocks.title: Characterisation of trees

blocks.body:
We prove that 1 and 2 are equivalent, the main statement; the other equivalences are left as exercises.

Step 1: a tree with $n \ge 2$ vertices has a leaf. Take a path $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_k$ of maximum length. Every neighbour of $v_0$ lies on the path, since otherwise the path could be extended. If $v_0$ were adjacent to some $v_i$ with $i \ge 2$, then $v_0, v_1, \dots, v_i, v_0$ would be a cycle. So $v_0$ has only the neighbour $v_1$, and is a leaf. (The same argument shows $v_k$ is a leaf, so there are at least two.)

Step 2: a tree on $n$ vertices has $n - 1$ edges (1 implies 2). Induct on $n$; for $n = 1$ there are no edges. For $n \ge 2$, delete a leaf and its edge. What remains is still connected (no path between two other vertices passes through a leaf) and still has no cycles, so it is a tree on $n-1$ vertices with $n-2$ edges by induction. Adding back the leaf gives $n - 1$ edges.

Step 3: every connected graph contains a spanning tree, that is a tree using all its vertices. While the graph has a cycle, delete one edge of that cycle; this keeps the graph connected. The number of edges drops each time, so the process stops, and the result is connected with no cycles.

Step 4 (2 implies 1). Let $G$ be connected with $n - 1$ edges. By Step 3 it contains a spanning tree $T$, and by Step 2, $T$ has $n - 1$ edges. So $T$ uses every edge of $G$, that is $G = T$, and $G$ is a tree.

blocks.title: Counting trees
blocks.body:
How many different trees can be built on the labelled vertex set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$? For $n = 3$ there are $3$ (choose the middle vertex), and for $n = 4$ there are $16$: the $12$ paths ($4!/2$ orderings) and the $4$ stars. Cayley's formula says the number is $n^{n-2}$ in general; a bijection due to Prüfer with sequences of length $n - 2$ from $\{1, \dots, n\}$ proves it, and is a good exercise in [[counting]].

By the handshake lemma, the degrees of a tree with $n \ge 2$ vertices add up to $2(n-1)$. The average degree is below $2$ and every degree is at least $1$, which is another way to see that leaves exist.

blocks.title: Euler tour
blocks.body:
An Euler tour of a multigraph is a closed trail that uses every edge exactly once. An Euler trail is a trail, not necessarily closed, that uses every edge exactly once.

In other words, you can draw the graph without lifting the pen or retracing a line, ending where you started (tour) or anywhere (trail).

blocks.title: Euler's theorem
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a multigraph with at least one edge, all of whose edges lie in a single connected component (isolated vertices are allowed). Then $G$ has an Euler tour if and only if every vertex has even degree. It has an Euler trail that is not closed if and only if exactly two vertices have odd degree; the trail then starts at one of them and ends at the other.

For a connected graph this is the statement: Euler tour exists $\iff$ connected and all degrees even.

Necessity. Each time an Euler tour passes through a vertex it enters along one edge and leaves along another, and the first and last edges pair up at the start. So the edge-ends at each vertex are split into pairs, and every degree is even.

Sufficiency. Suppose all degrees are even. First a key observation: if we start at a vertex $v$ and walk along unused edges for as long as possible, we can only get stuck at $v$. Indeed, think of each edge as having two ends (a loop has both ends at the same vertex), so that $\deg w$ is the number of edge-ends at $w$. Each time the walk arrives at a vertex $w \ne v$, it has used an odd number of edge-ends at $w$: arrivals and departures at $w$ alternate, every earlier departure was matched with an earlier arrival, and the current arrival is unmatched. Since $\deg w$ is even, some edge-end at $w$ is unused, and its edge is unused (a used edge has both ends used). So the walk can leave $w$.

Now let $T$ be a closed trail with as many edges as possible; one exists, since by the observation a walk from any vertex with an edge ends where it began. Suppose $T$ misses some edge $xy$. Because all edges lie in one component, there is a walk that starts at a vertex of $T$, travels to $x$, and then uses the edge $xy$. Its first edge that is not in $T$ starts at a vertex $u$ that lies on $T$, so $u$ is a vertex of $T$ with an unused edge. In the multigraph of unused edges every degree is still even, since $T$ uses an even number of edges at each vertex. Start at $u$ in the unused edges and walk as long as possible; by the observation the walk is a closed trail $T'$ returning to $u$. Inserting $T'$ into $T$ at $u$ gives a longer closed trail, a contradiction. So $T$ is an Euler tour.

For the trail version with odd vertices $a$ and $b$, add a new edge $ab$; now all degrees are even, take an Euler tour, and delete the new edge. Conversely an open Euler trail pairs the edges at every vertex except its two ends, which therefore have odd degree.

blocks.title: Handshakes
blocks.body: Can each of $9$ people shake hands with exactly $3$ of the others? And can each of $10$ people do so?
blocks.solution:
Make the people vertices and the handshakes edges. With $9$ people, the degrees would add up to $9 \cdot 3 = 27$, which is odd, contradicting the handshake lemma. So it is impossible.

With $10$ people it is possible. Seat them around a round table and let everyone shake hands with both neighbours and with the person directly opposite. Each person gets exactly $3$ handshakes, $15$ in total, and indeed $2 \cdot 15 = 30 = 10 \cdot 3$.

blocks.title: How many leaves?
blocks.body:
Show that in every tree with at least two vertices,
$$\#\{\text{leaves}\} = 2 + \sum_{v:\ \deg v \ge 3} (\deg v - 2).$$
A tree has only vertices of degree $1$ and $3$, ten of them of degree $3$. How many leaves does it have?
blocks.solution:
Let $n$ be the number of vertices. In a tree with $n \ge 2$ vertices no vertex has degree $0$, since the tree is connected. The handshake lemma and the tree theorem give $\sum_v \deg v = 2(n-1)$, which we can rewrite as $\sum_v (\deg v - 2) = -2$. Vertices of degree $2$ contribute $0$, leaves contribute $-1$ each, and the others contribute $\deg v - 2$. So
$$-\#\{\text{leaves}\} + \sum_{\deg v \ge 3}(\deg v - 2) = -2,$$
which is the formula.

For the second question each degree-$3$ vertex contributes $1$, so the number of leaves is $2 + 10 = 12$. Check: $n = 22$ vertices, degree sum $12 + 30 = 42 = 2 \cdot 21$.

blocks.title: The bridges and the dominoes
blocks.body:
(a) Königsberg had four land areas: an island joined to the other areas by $5$ bridges, and three areas each touched by $3$ bridges, $7$ bridges in all. Is there a walk crossing every bridge exactly once?

(b) A standard set of dominoes has one tile for each unordered pair $\{a, b\}$ with $0 \le a \le b \le 6$ ($28$ tiles). Can all of them be laid in a closed ring, touching ends matching? What about the set with numbers $0$ to $7$ ($36$ tiles)?
blocks.solution:
(a) Make a multigraph with a vertex for each land area and an edge for each bridge. The degrees are $5, 3, 3, 3$ (sum $14 = 2 \cdot 7$). All four are odd, but an Euler trail allows at most two odd vertices. So no such walk exists, which is what Euler showed in 1736.

(b) Make the numbers $0, \dots, 6$ vertices and each tile $\{a, b\}$ an edge ($a = b$ gives a loop). A ring of tiles with matching ends is exactly an Euler tour. Each vertex $a$ lies on the $6$ edges to the other numbers and on one loop, so its degree is $6 + 2 = 8$, which is even. The multigraph is connected, so a ring exists.

With numbers $0$ to $7$ every vertex has degree $7 + 2 = 9$. All eight vertices are odd, so there is no ring, and not even an open line of all $36$ tiles (that would need at most two odd vertices).

blocks.body:
- Both conditions in 'connected with $n - 1$ edges' are needed. A triangle together with one isolated vertex has $4$ vertices and $3$ edges but is not a tree; a path on $4$ vertices plus an extra edge is connected but has a cycle.
- Euler's criterion needs the edges to lie in one component. Two disjoint triangles have all degrees even but no Euler tour. Isolated vertices, on the other hand, do no harm.
- Proofs often go wrong by treating a walk as if it could not repeat vertices.
- An Euler tour uses every edge once. A cycle through every vertex once is a Hamiltonian cycle, a much harder notion with no simple criterion (see [[cycles-matchings]]).

Graphs are the common language for the rest of combinatorics. Hamiltonian cycles and matchings are developed in [[cycles-matchings]], and colourings in [[graph-coloring]]. How many edges force a given subgraph is [[extremal-graphs]], and what any colouring of the edges must contain is [[ramsey]]. Allowing edges with more than two ends gives [[hypergraphs]].

On the computational side, connectivity and Euler tours can be decided in time linear in the size of the graph, while deciding whether a Hamiltonian cycle exists is NP-complete; that contrast is a good entry point to [[p-vs-np]].

1. Prove that every graph with at least two vertices has two vertices of the same degree.
2. Prove that a graph with $n$ vertices and at least $n$ edges contains a cycle.
3. A connected graph has exactly $2k$ vertices of odd degree, with $k \ge 1$. Show that its edges can be split into $k$ trails, and not fewer.
4. Complete the proof of the tree theorem by showing that conditions 3 and 4 are each equivalent to condition 1.
